true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end check uses the slot start time

The end variable is calculated from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime. This lets events extend past a host's working-hours boundary as long as their start is inside it. In particular, when another host's date override generates additional candidates, a fixed host working until 11:00 can pass this check for a 10:30–11:30 event. Compare the actual event end against the working interval's end.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

false_positives.candidate:
Date overrides bypass calendar and booking conflicts

When a slot falls on a date with an override, checkIfIsAvailable returns true before evaluating the host's busy intervals. An override defines working availability; it does not make existing bookings or calendar events available. Consequently, both fixed and round-robin hosts can be offered for slots that conflict with existing commitments. Accepted override slots must still pass the busy-time check.

Timezone conversion drops overrides that cross attendee midnight

The converted override endpoints are reduced to hour/minute values, discarding their dates. An override from 22:00–23:00 UTC viewed in UTC+1 becomes startTime 1380 and endTime 0. buildSlots treats that as an invalid range and produces no slots, although 23:00–00:00 is valid availability. Preserve the converted day boundaries and split ranges at attendee midnight instead of wrapping the end back to zero.

Working-hours validation rejects valid split schedules

The workingHours.find predicate rejects a slot if it is outside any working interval for the weekday, rather than accepting it if it fits one interval. With ordinary split availability of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, a 10:00 slot is rejected for being outside the afternoon interval, and a 14:00 slot is rejected for being outside the morning interval. This removes all available slots for such hosts. Validate membership in at least one applicable interval instead; a weekday with no applicable intervals should also be unavailable.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Handle integrations without sender metadata

The new check unconditionally indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"], but sender is optional in build_integration, and the basic installation flow in this file's tests explicitly creates metadata without it. If such an Integration remains after its OrganizationIntegration is removed, attempting to attach it again now raises KeyError and returns a server error instead of completing or displaying the invalid-installation message. Handle missing sender metadata explicitly and obtain trustworthy installer information if it is required.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Compare immutable GitHub user IDs instead of logins

The ownership check compares the current OAuth user's login with the login stored in the installation webhook. GitHub usernames can be changed and subsequently claimed by another account, so these strings do not reliably identify the same user. After the installer renames their account, the legitimate installer is rejected, while a different account claiming the old username can pass verification for an unlinked installation. Store and compare the immutable GitHub user ID from both responses instead.

Do not bypass installer verification when the integration is missing

When no Integration row exists for the supplied installation_id, this branch advances the pipeline without checking the authenticated GitHub user against the installer. build_integration then retrieves that installation using app credentials, which does not establish that the OAuth user has access to it. A user who supplies another installation's ID before its installation webhook has created the Integration row can therefore attach it to their Sentry organization. The missing-row path needs to fail closed or independently verify ownership rather than skipping the new security check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Generate the queued timestamp per AssignmentSource instance

`timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value receives the same worker-startup timestamp. Consequently, the `queued` metadata serialized into outbound tasks does not represent when those assignments were queued and can be arbitrarily stale in long-running workers. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` to generate a fresh timestamp for each instance.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Keep the registered metric-alert handler instantiable

MetricAlertDetectorHandler now inherits StatefulDetectorHandler but implements none of its abstract members: counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data. It therefore cannot be instantiated. Accessing detector.detector_handler for the registered metric_alert_fire type raises TypeError, causing process_detectors to abort rather than returning the previous empty result. Keep a concrete no-op handler until these methods are implemented, or implement the required methods before registering this stateful handler.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

false_positives.candidate:
Build the expected occurrence with the group key being evaluated

TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds its expected occurrence using group key "val1", but calls evaluate_group_key_value with "group_key". The helper includes that key in the occurrence fingerprint, so the expected occurrence has fingerprint "<detector_id>:val1" while the handler correctly produces "<detector_id>:group_key". This is an incorrect expected result for the new occurrence-generation path; construct the expected occurrence with "group_key" so the assertion checks the occurrence belonging to the evaluated group.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawned workers fail the multiprocessing.Process type check

Workers are created using multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, whose SpawnProcess class is not a subclass of the default-context multiprocessing.Process class. Consequently, this isinstance check is false for production workers, so an unhealthy worker is never killed before its replacement starts. A hung worker that later resumes can flush the same shards concurrently with its replacement. The identical check in join() also prevents terminating workers that exceed the shutdown timeout. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or explicitly distinguish threads from spawned processes in both places.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Shutdown skips remaining workers when the shared deadline expires

When the join deadline expires, this break skips every remaining worker without attempting to terminate it. With multiple flusher processes, one worker blocked on Redis or Kafka can consume the entire timeout, leaving other blocked workers alive after join() returns. During rebalancing, those workers can outlive their partition assignment and overlap with new flushers. Stop waiting once the deadline expires, but still perform termination cleanup for every worker.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Bound queued work and propagate backpressure

Every worker queue is created with the default maxsize=0, which makes it unbounded, and submit always accepts more work. If processing is slower than Kafka ingestion, or a worker is blocked on a slow result, the consumer continues accumulating decoded results, original Kafka messages, and offset-tracking entries in memory without limit. This can exhaust the consumer's memory instead of applying the advertised backpressure. Use bounded capacity and signal Arroyo to retry submissions when capacity is exhausted.

Create a fresh queue pool for each processing strategy

The factory creates one queue pool in its constructor and reuses it for every create_with_partitions call, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close shuts that pool down. Arroyo closes and recreates strategies when partition assignments change, so after the first rebalance the new strategy receives queues whose workers have stopped and whose queues have been shut down. Submissions then fail and the submit exception handler marks those messages completed, allowing unprocessed results to be committed. The pool and its offset tracker need a lifecycle scoped to each strategy rather than being reused after shutdown.

Do not acknowledge messages when submission fails

The broad submit exception handler treats any decoding, grouping, or enqueueing exception as successful completion by adding and immediately completing the message's offset. For example, if build_payload_grouping_key raises or work_queue.put fails because the queue is shut down, the result was never handed to a worker but the next commit can advance past it permanently. Expected invalid-payload handling already has the decoder's None path; unexpected submission failures should propagate or remain pending rather than acknowledge unprocessed results.

Drain accepted work and commit completion before graceful shutdown

close stops the commit loop before shutting down the pool, and pool shutdown sets every worker's shutdown flag before draining its queue. Consequently, queued results are abandoned and results completed during worker shutdown are never included in a final commit. join simply calls close again and ignores its timeout, so it does not provide Arroyo's graceful draining phase either. On shutdown or rebalance this causes accepted work to be replayed, including already-applied results; workers that exceed the fixed five-second join can also keep applying old results after processing resumes elsewhere. Separate closing submissions from draining workers, honor the join timeout, and commit the final completed offsets after draining.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Seed an actual grant in the denial-precedence test

The test says it grants dashboard access to prove that the denial entry takes precedence, but it stores `"dashboards:uid:dash1": false`. checkPermission treats that entry as a denial, so this does not test the intended conflict between a cached grant and a cached denial. Set the entry to true so the test verifies that a denial-cache hit overrides an otherwise allowed request.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Encode denial-key components without delimiter collisions

Concatenating resource name and parent with unescaped underscores allows different requests to share a denial key. For the same namespace, subject, and action, name `foo_bar` with parent `baz` collides with name `foo` and parent `bar_baz`. Underscores are supported in legacy dashboard/folder UIDs, and request validation does not exclude them. A denial for one resource can therefore incorrectly deny access to another resource for the cache TTL. Use an unambiguous encoding of the components.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Include the identity type in denial-cache keys

The denial key uses only the parsed subject ID, discarding IdentityType even though permission lookup distinguishes anonymous, renderer, and user identities. For example, `anonymous:0` and `render:0` produce the same denial key for the same dashboard request. If the anonymous request is denied first, the renderer request is also denied for 30 seconds without reaching getRendererPermissions, which would grant dashboard read access. Include the identity type in the key to prevent denials from crossing identity boundaries.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence notifications is a no-op for Prometheus-only list items

GrafanaRuleListItem now calls this component without rule, and AlertRuleMenu can display Silence notifications using promRule permissions. Clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer to true, but the drawer is still rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. With rule undefined that condition is always false, so no drawer opens. Load the required ruler data on demand or adapt the drawer to accept the Prometheus rule before exposing this action.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

false_positives.candidate:
Grafana recording rules lose the Export menu action

The Prometheus-based ModifyExport ability is supported only for alerting rules. The previous ruler-based ability used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule, which includes Grafana recording rules as well. Since the new Grafana list items no longer supply rulerRule, recording rules now have no supported export ability and their Export menu disappears even for users with read permission. Use the Grafana-rule check rather than the alerting-only check for this action to retain recording-rule export.

Pause and Delete disappear from Grafana rule list menus

The new list item supplies only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, but AlertRuleMenu still requires a Grafana rulerRule to render Pause and requires rulerRule to render Delete. Computing the Prometheus-based abilities does not remove those rendering guards. Consequently, even users with update and delete permissions can no longer pause, resume, or delete Grafana-managed rules from the new list. These actions need handlers and rendering paths that work with the Prometheus rule identifier.

Preserve the immutability check for federated rule groups

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously checked isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), but it now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, where isFederated is hardcoded to false. Existing CombinedRule consumers therefore lose the protection that disables Update and Delete for Mimir federated groups with source_tenants. Users with external write permissions are now offered editing and deletion of rules that this UI previously treated as immutable. Preserve the group-level federation information when delegating rather than dropping this existing restriction.

The skip token still grants Grafana duplicate abilities

Passing skipToken converts the rule to undefined but does not disable the returned abilities. For an undefined rule, useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities treats duplication as supported and allows it whenever the user has Grafana rule-create permission. AlertRuleMenu calls this hook with skipToken for data-source-managed rules and ORs its result with the ruler abilities. This can expose Duplicate for external rules whose ruler does not support it, or for plugin-provided external rules whose duplication was explicitly disabled. Return disabled abilities when the hook is skipped rather than evaluating an absent rule as a supported Grafana rule.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Avoid interpolating shard queries a second time in runSplitQuery

Queries interpolated here are subsequently passed to runSplitQuery, which now calls applyTemplateVariables again for every shard batch. Template interpolation is not idempotent when a variable's value contains variable-like text. For example, if a service variable has the literal value `$other`, the first pass correctly produces a selector containing that value, but the second pass expands `$other` if that variable exists, querying a different service. Keep the early interpolation needed for shard selection, but ensure runSplitQuery can accept already-interpolated targets without applying template variables again. The updated test asserting five interpolation calls currently enshrines this double-processing rather than preventing it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Preserve the test logger's recorder in FromContext

FromContext returns a fresh TestLogger with independent log storage. LoggerMiddleware now emits every request-completion log through logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so injecting a TestLogger records those calls on an inaccessible temporary instance while the supplied logger's InfoLogs remains empty. Tests inspecting the injected logger can no longer observe request logging. Return the existing fake, or share its recording state with the contextual logger.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device counting and admission are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices in one database session and performs the insert in a separate session without locking or another atomic admission mechanism. If the count is one below deviceLimit, concurrent requests for different new devices can all observe the available slot and all insert successfully. This also occurs across Grafana instances sharing the database, allowing the active device count to exceed the configured limit; subsequent updates continue admitting those excess devices. Serialize the count-and-admit operation at the database level and add a concurrent admission test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected devices are cached as successfully admitted

TagDevice now propagates the limit error to authentication, but tagDeviceUI still inserts the device into localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, that cache entry remains for 29 minutes. A second request with the same device ID hits the cache and returns nil, so Authenticate grants anonymous access despite the limit. Concurrent requests can bypass the check even before the first store call completes. Cache only successfully admitted devices, and ensure in-flight checks cannot be treated as successful admissions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Omitting the device header bypasses the configured limit

Authenticate enforces the limit solely through TagDevice, but TagDevice returns nil without consulting the store when X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent. Consequently, an unauthenticated client can omit that header and continue accessing anonymous APIs even when device_limit is exhausted. The configured limit needs an admission policy for requests without a device ID, rather than treating skipped tracking as successful admission.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors

The new cleanup paths emit Error logs for every successful SELECT and DELETE, including empty batches, with a nil error. Orphan-tag cleanup runs even when annotation retention is disabled, so normal scheduled cleanup now produces recurring false error reports. This can trigger log-based alerts and obscure actual failures; log successful operations at Debug level and reserve Error for failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Keep the shared cleanup cadence unchanged

Changing this ticker from ten minutes to one minute accelerates every cleanup job, not just annotation cleanup. Temporary-file directory scans, snapshot and dashboard-version deletion, image cleanup, invite expiration, and query-history retention now run ten times as often, increasing filesystem and database load independently of the deadlock fix. The shared cleanup timeout is still nine minutes, so slow cleanup passes can also leave a tick pending and run again immediately. Keep the existing cadence unless this broader scheduling change is separately justified.

false_positives.candidate:
Bound parameterized deletes by the database parameter limit

The non-SQLite branch creates one bound parameter per selected ID without capping the batch. MySQL prepared statements and PostgreSQL's parameter protocol support at most 65,535 parameters, so an annotation cleanup batch configured above that limit fails whenever enough eligible rows exist. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not have this restriction. Split the selected IDs into supported-size deletes or otherwise avoid exceeding the backend's parameter limit.

Build the SQLite ID list without repeatedly copying its entire prefix

For SQLite batches above 999, each iteration formats the entire accumulated ID list into a new string. Building a batch of N IDs therefore takes quadratic copying and allocation rather than linear work. Configured batches containing tens of thousands of IDs can allocate gigabytes of temporary strings, causing substantial GC pressure and delaying cleanup and other work. Use strings.Builder or a byte buffer to append each ID once.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Attribute operation durations to the store that was called

DeleteCollection records its asynchronous legacy operation with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are reported as unified-storage observations. Conversely, the Create and Update unified-storage error paths at lines 45 and 129 call recordLegacyDuration even though legacy is not called. These mistakes hide failures in the actual store and incorrectly inflate the other store's metrics. Use recordLegacyDuration for the legacy collection deletion and recordStorageDuration for unified Create/Update failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Do not use object names as the metric kind label

The successful Delete metric passes name where the other duration calls pass options.Kind. This creates a separate Prometheus label value for every deleted object instead of a bounded resource kind, causing unbounded metric-series growth as objects are deleted and making successful and failed delete metrics inconsistent. Pass options.Kind here.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Detach background writes from request cancellation

The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. HTTP request contexts are canceled when the handler returns, so returning the unified-storage result can cancel the legacy write before it starts or while it is running; the ten-second timeout does not prevent parent cancellation. The same problem affects Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Preserve the necessary context values but detach cancellation before applying the background timeout so successful requests actually replicate to legacy storage.

Preserve write ordering when replicating asynchronously

Each successful mutation launches an independent goroutine with no ordering between legacy operations. Even sequential client requests can therefore be applied out of order: a create followed by a delete can execute the legacy delete first and then leave the deleted object present in legacy, while two updates can leave the older value last. Since legacy is intended as a safety copy, replication needs an ordered mechanism for conflicting writes rather than independent goroutines.

Replicate the committed update result instead of replaying objInfo

The legacy Update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the updateWrapper containing the object committed by unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a PATCH or server-side apply transformation that depends on the existing object. Re-evaluating it against legacy's potentially stale object can produce a different result—for example, preserving fields that an earlier unified update changed but that have not yet reached legacy. Pass a snapshot of the successful unified update result through the wrapper so legacy receives the same desired object rather than recomputing the request against a different base.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock

Concurrent non-development calls that observe an empty cache all proceed to acquire the write lock. After the first call populates the cache, each queued call still reloads and parses the manifest while holding the exclusive lock instead of using the cached result. A burst of requests at startup therefore causes repeated, serialized file reads and blocks otherwise cacheable requests behind those reloads. Recheck entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock and return it when populated outside development mode.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Preserve per-key serialization while building indexes

BuildIndex now locks only when publishing the completed index, so GetIndex returns nil throughout an in-progress build. Concurrent searches, or a search and a write-event handler, can therefore build separate indexes for the same namespace/group/resource. For memory indexes, one completed index can receive watch updates and then be replaced in the cache by another build that did not include those updates, leaving search results stale. File-backed builds also compete to create the same directory and can fail. parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the safeParse wrapper { success: true, data: ... }, unlike the previous googleCredentialSchema.parse call, which returned the credentials themselves. Saving this wrapper as Credential.key removes access_token and the other expected fields from the top level. After any successful refresh, including with syncing disabled, the next GoogleCalendarService construction fails googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key). Persist the parsed data rather than the wrapper.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
The sync branch returns a different response type from SDK refreshes

The sync branch returns an unparsed fetch Response, but several callers expect their refresh callback's SDK-specific return value. Google reads res.data, Zoho CRM and Bigin read tokenInfo.data, and HubSpot reads accessToken/expiresIn directly. A fetch Response has none of those fields, so enabling syncing causes these integrations to throw or use undefined tokens even when the endpoint returns valid JSON. Normalize and decode the sync response into the contract expected by each caller.

false_positives.candidate:
Import Prisma before using the new credential update

The new refresh path calls prisma.credential.update, but this file has no prisma import or declaration. This fails TypeScript checking and, if executed without checking, throws ReferenceError after Salesforce successfully returns a token. Import the Prisma client used by the other integration services.

Salesforce refresh bypasses the configured credential-sync endpoint

The new Salesforce refresh unconditionally posts to Salesforce rather than using refreshOAuthTokens. Thus, even with credential sharing and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT configured, Cal.com independently refreshes the provider token and requires a locally stored refresh token. An external app store supplying only an access token cannot keep this integration working, and it is not the source of truth for refreshes as it is for the other integrations. Route this refresh through the sync helper.

Use the installed Zoom app slug in sync requests

The refresh request sends appSlug="zoomvideo", while the Zoom OAuth callback creates credentials with appId="zoom" and the new webhook resolves applications by their actual slug. A parent app store using that same slug to look up credentials cannot resolve this refresh request. Send "zoom" consistently with the credential and webhook contracts.

The advertised minimal sync response is incompatible with provider parsers

The helper says the sync endpoint should return only an access token and expiry, but its fetch-based callers still require provider-specific response structures. Webex validates scope, token_type, refresh_token and refresh_token_expires_in; Lark requires a success code and nested data containing refresh-token expiry fields. An endpoint implementing the stated minimal contract cannot refresh either integration. Add adapters that merge the minimal response with existing credentials, or define and document the provider-specific contract actually required.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Await reminder cancellation before completing the booking cancellation

The reminder helpers now perform the database update or deletion themselves, but their returned promises are discarded by the nested forEach calls. Previously, database reminder deletions were included in the awaited Promise.all. The handler can now report a successful cancellation while its cancelled flags or unscheduled-reminder deletions are still pending; in a serverless request those operations can be interrupted after the response, leaving reminders eligible to be sent. Collect and await these helper promises, including the equivalent requestReschedule calls.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: asynchronous reminder deletion functions (helpers) are called inside `forEach` loops without awaiting their promises during booking cancellation/rescheduling, which can cause reminders to remain active instead of being properly cancelled.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancel imminent reminders without waiting for the cron job

Scheduled emails are now only marked cancelled, even when their send time is before the next 15-minute cron run. For example, an email due at 10:10 for a booking cancelled at 10:01 after the 10:00 run will still be sent. At 10:15, scheduleEmailReminders deletes the expired reminder before attempting cancellation, so it never contacts SendGrid for that email. Reminders close to their send time need an immediate cancellation path.

Do not bypass deferred cancellation for every reschedule

Passing immediateDelete=true cancels every old rescheduled-booking email immediately in SendGrid, including emails scheduled days ahead. Those cancellations remain pending until their original send dates and consume the same 100-pending-cancellation limit identified in this PR. Once that limit is reached, the helper catches the failure without setting cancelled=true, leaving the old reminder scheduled with no cron retry. Rescheduling therefore still exhausts the cancellation quota and sends obsolete reminders.

Isolate cancellation failures and persist each successful cancellation

The entire cancellation loop shares one try/catch, and its Prisma deletes are lazy promises executed only after every SendGrid request succeeds. If any request fails, all later reminders are skipped and none of the earlier successful cancellations are removed from the database. A persistent failure can consequently block unrelated cancellations on every run until their emails are sent. Handle errors per reminder and execute each database deletion after its corresponding successful cancellation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

Update calendars using the booking organizer's credentials

The handler allows attendees and team administrators to add guests, but constructs EventManager with the caller and the caller's credentials. When the caller is not the booking organizer, those credentials do not authorize updates to the organizer's existing calendar event. Guests are already persisted before this update is attempted, so the booking can gain attendees while the actual calendar invitation remains unchanged or the mutation fails. Handle seated bookings through the seat allocation flow

This mutation accepts seated bookings but inserts ordinary attendees without checking seatsPerTimeSlot or creating seat references. The new action is also exposed for these bookings. As a result, callers can add attendees beyond the configured capacity, and those attendees have no seat reference for the seat-specific cancellation and rescheduling links used by the booking UI. The handler checks permissions and guest addresses but never checks the booking status. An authorized caller can invoke it for a cancelled or rejected booking, after which new guests receive AttendeeScheduledEmail and existing attendees receive an ICS request marked CONFIRMED. false_positives.candidate:
Preserve credential IDs on video references

This change sets credentialId to undefined for every non-calendar result, discarding the credential ID returned by video meeting creation. handleCancelBooking only deletes a video meeting when its booking reference has a credentialId. Initialize the destination array before adding collective hosts

If neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, evt.destinationCalendar is initialized to null. The optional push then silently discards all destination calendars collected from the other collective hosts. Those hosts receive no calendar events even when their calendars are connected. Initialize an empty array and append the collected destinations regardless of whether the organizer has one.

Retain destination selection for calendars without a credential ID

EventManager explicitly supports destination calendars without a credentialId by invoking the credentials matching their integration. This new lookup cannot match such a destination to the numeric credentialId passed to createEvent, so Google always inserts into primary rather than the configured externalId. Existing destinations using that fallback will start putting bookings in the wrong calendar. Preserve the legacy selection when the destination has no credentialId.

Cancel recurring events using each reference's credential

In the allRemainingBookings branch, the credential resolved for the current host is discarded. The code instead loops only over the booking owner's credentials and selects the first calendar reference from each recurring booking. With multiple collective hosts, this repeats deletion of the first host's events while never deleting the other hosts' events, despite marking every booking cancelled. The additional collective destinations assembled in handleNewBooking are not persisted on the booking, and this handler does not reload them. Create a fresh queue pool for each processing strategy

The factory creates one queue pool in its constructor and reuses it for every create_with_partitions call, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close shuts that pool down. Arroyo closes and recreates strategies when partition assignments change, so after the first rebalance the new strategy receives queues whose workers have stopped and whose queues have been shut down. Submissions then fail and the submit exception handler marks those messages completed, allowing unprocessed results to be committed. The pool and its offset tracker need a lifecycle scoped to each strategy rather than being reused after shutdown.

Every worker queue is created with the default maxsize=0, which makes it unbounded, and submit always accepts more work. If processing is slower than Kafka ingestion, or a worker is blocked on a slow result, the consumer continues accumulating decoded results, original Kafka messages, and offset-tracking entries in memory without limit. This can exhaust the consumer's memory instead of applying the advertised backpressure. Use bounded capacity and signal Arroyo to retry submissions when capacity is exhausted.

Drain accepted work and commit completion before graceful shutdown

close stops the commit loop before shutting down the pool, and pool shutdown sets every worker's shutdown flag before draining its queue. Consequently, queued results are abandoned and results completed during worker shutdown are never included in a final commit. join simply calls close again and ignores its timeout, so it does not provide Arroyo's graceful draining phase either. On shutdown or rebalance this causes accepted work to be replayed, including already-applied results; workers that exceed the fixed five-second join can also keep applying old results after processing resumes elsewhere. Separate closing submissions from draining workers, honor the join timeout, and commit the final completed offsets after draining.

Do not acknowledge messages when submission fails

The broad submit exception handler treats any decoding, grouping, or enqueueing exception as successful completion by adding and immediately completing the message's offset. For example, if build_payload_grouping_key raises or work_queue.put fails because the queue is shut down, the result was never handed to a worker but the next commit can advance past it permanently. Expected invalid-payload handling already has the decoder's None path; unexpected submission failures should propagate or remain pending rather than acknowledge unprocessed results.

false_positives.candidate:
Changing existing Redis keys from sets to sorted sets requires a migration

The buffer now uses ZADD and ZSCAN on the same span-buf:s:* keys that the previous version populated with SADD. Any buffered segment present during deployment remains a Redis set, so new insertions and flushing those segments fail with WRONGTYPE. Mixed-version consumers also cannot read or write each other's buffers. Provide a compatible conversion or a versioned-key rollout that drains the old buffers before switching; otherwise deployment stalls processing of existing data.

Unioning sorted sets must preserve timestamps rather than sum them

ZUNIONSTORE defaults to AGGREGATE SUM. A replayed span can exist both in the destination buffer and in a newly staged parent buffer when that parent has already been redirected. Merging those buffers doubles the duplicate payload's end-timestamp score, although its actual timestamp has not changed. Subsequent ZPOPMIN eviction then retains these replayed old spans ahead of genuinely newer spans. Use an aggregation mode such as MAX so merging duplicate payloads preserves their timestamp.

Insertion eviction ignores the configured segment span limit

SpansBuffer still accepts and stores max_segment_spans, but the Python span-count check was removed and this script unconditionally caps every segment at 1000. A caller configuring a smaller limit now receives segments exceeding that limit, while a larger configured limit silently loses spans at 1000. Pass the configured limit to the insertion script and use it for eviction, or explicitly remove the configurable contract rather than leaving it ineffective.

Check upsampling against the dataset actually being queried

The eligibility check uses the outer `dataset`, while query execution uses `scoped_dataset`. These differ in the dashboard splitting paths: a metrics-enhanced request can execute an error-only query against Discover, but this check still sees the metrics dataset and rejects upsampling. As a result, sampled error charts produced by those paths continue to report stored counts rather than estimated counts. Pass the actual scoped dataset and effective query into the eligibility check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset. In the dashboard split path, metrics becomes discover, so upsampling is wrongly skipped. The candidate's extra note about passing the effective query does not change the core issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Parse the query instead of using a substring to identify error-only searches

The presence of `event.type:error` does not mean a Discover query selects only errors. For example, `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` and `!event.type:error` both pass this check. For allowlisted projects, their count is then replaced with an aggregation over `sample_weight`, even though the helper explicitly states that transactions do not have that field. These valid searches can consequently fail or return incorrect counts. Determine whether the parsed query actually restricts results to errors before applying the transformation.

Apply weighted counting to top-event selection as well as its time series

For top-events requests, only `timeseries_columns` is transformed to weighted counting; `selected_columns` and `orderby` are still passed directly from the original request. A request selecting and ordering by `count()` therefore chooses its top groups using stored-event counts, then plots weighted counts for those groups. With differing client sample rates, a group with fewer stored events can have the largest estimated count and still be excluded from the chart. Transform the selection and ranking aggregates consistently with the time-series aggregate.

Include the identity type in the key to prevent denials from crossing identity boundaries.

The ownership check compares the current OAuth user's login with the login stored in the installation webhook. GitHub usernames can be changed and subsequently claimed by another account, so these strings do not reliably identify the same user. After the installer renames their account, the legitimate installer is rejected, while a different account claiming the old username can pass verification for an unlinked installation. false_positives.candidate:
Compare stored login eligibility rather than organization-aware enabled state

The original model passed here comes from getById(), which wraps isEnabled() to return false when its organization is disabled (or organizations are disabled for the realm). The login query, however, selects IDs using the stored enabled flag. If a public, enabled organization IdP is already cached, its organization is disabled, and the IdP is then made hidden-on-login or link-only, both predicates here return false and invalidation is skipped. Re-enabling the organization leaves that IdP in the login cache; OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only rechecks isEnabled(), so it displays the now-hidden or link-only provider. Compare the original persisted eligibility flags without the organization-aware wrapper when deciding whether query membership changed.

Do not merge an old query after a concurrent invalidation

When an organization search is missing, this branch carries all results from the previously read query into a replacement tagged with a freshly obtained revision and current counter. A concurrent transaction can change an IdP's login eligibility or organization and invalidate the login cache after this request reads query but before invalidateObject() runs. The replacement then reinstates the old organization's stale ID set under the new revision, even though only the newly requested organization's results were reloaded. Subsequent logins can omit newly eligible providers or display hidden/link-only providers until another invalidation. Rebuild without the old query when its revision is no longer current, and ensure a concurrent invalidation cannot be bypassed by stamping stale results with the current counter.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. After the first call populates the cache, each queued call still reloads and parses the manifest while holding the exclusive lock instead of using the cached result. A burst of requests at startup therefore causes repeated, serialized file reads and blocks otherwise cacheable requests behind those reloads. Recheck entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock and return it when populated outside development mode.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

false_positives.candidate:
Build the SQLite ID list without repeatedly copying its entire prefix

For SQLite batches above 999, each iteration formats the entire accumulated ID list into a new string. Building a batch of N IDs therefore takes quadratic copying and allocation rather than linear work. Configured batches containing tens of thousands of IDs can allocate gigabytes of temporary strings, causing substantial GC pressure and delaying cleanup and other work. Use strings.Builder or a byte buffer to append each ID once.

Bound parameterized deletes by the database parameter limit

The non-SQLite branch creates one bound parameter per selected ID without capping the batch. MySQL prepared statements and PostgreSQL's parameter protocol support at most 65,535 parameters, so an annotation cleanup batch configured above that limit fails whenever enough eligible rows exist. The previous subquery-based DELETE did not have this restriction. Split the selected IDs into supported-size deletes or otherwise avoid exceeding the backend's parameter limit.

Conversely, the Create and Update unified-storage error paths at lines 45 and 129 call recordLegacyDuration even though legacy is not called. These mistakes hide failures in the actual store and incorrectly inflate the other store's metrics. Use recordLegacyDuration for the legacy collection deletion and recordStorageDuration for unified Create/Update failures.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag swapped duration-metric functions in DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection. The direction differs: the golden says the storage failure path wrongly calls recordLegacyDuration. The candidate says the legacy operation wrongly calls recordStorageDuration. It then applies the golden's exact pattern to Create and Update instead. This is the same underlying misattribution bug in the same method, but not precisely the same line.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Do not use object names as the metric kind label

The successful Delete metric passes name where the other duration calls pass options.Kind. This creates a separate Prometheus label value for every deleted object instead of a bounded resource kind, causing unbounded metric-series growth as objects are deleted and making successful and failed delete metrics inconsistent. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: metrics recording uses name instead of options.Kind, which is inconsistent with the other methods. The candidate also mentions the cardinality impact, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Detach background writes from request cancellation

The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. HTTP request contexts are canceled when the handler returns, so returning the unified-storage result can cancel the legacy write before it starts or while it is running; the ten-second timeout does not prevent parent cancellation. The same problem affects Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Preserve the necessary context values but detach cancellation before applying the background timeout so successful requests actually replicate to legacy storage.

Preserve write ordering when replicating asynchronously

Each successful mutation launches an independent goroutine with no ordering between legacy operations. Even sequential client requests can therefore be applied out of order: a create followed by a delete can execute the legacy delete first and then leave the deleted object present in legacy, while two updates can leave the older value last. Since legacy is intended as a safety copy, replication needs an ordered mechanism for conflicting writes rather than independent goroutines.

Replicate the committed update result instead of replaying objInfo

The legacy Update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the updateWrapper containing the object committed by unified storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a PATCH or server-side apply transformation that depends on the existing object. Re-evaluating it against legacy's potentially stale object can produce a different result—for example, preserving fields that an earlier unified update changed but that have not yet reached legacy. Pass a snapshot of the successful unified update result through the wrapper so legacy receives the same desired object rather than recomputing the request against a different base.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

Increment the retry counter atomically

Both failure paths write `reminder.retryCount + 1` using the value fetched before processing the batch. If two cron invocations overlap and both fail to schedule the same reminder, they can both read 0 and write 1, losing one failure. The reminder then survives despite having failed twice and receives additional scheduling attempts. Use Prisma's atomic increment operation in both failure paths rather than assigning a value from the stale snapshot.

false_positives.candidate:

If the reminder has been deleted while scheduling was in progress (for example, by an overlapping cron's expired-reminder cleanup), Prisma's update throws because the row no longer exists. A database outage can likewise make both the original update and this recovery update fail. That exception escapes the per-reminder catch, aborting the handler and leaving every remaining reminder in the batch unprocessed; previously the catch logged the error and continued. true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

Office365CalendarService accepts refresh responses without a new refresh token and merges parsed fields into its existing credentials; this new dummy field overwrites the valid stored refresh token. The next refresh then sends the dummy value to Microsoft and fails. Preserve the existing refresh token when the provider does not return a replacement.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: when the response omits refresh_token, the code inserts the literal string 'refresh_token' as a dummy value. That overwrites the valid token and breaks the next refresh.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

Using a Zod schema's toString() as a computed property name does not create a wildcard validator. These properties become literal keys (normally "[object Object]"), and z.object strips unrecognized fields. With credential sharing enabled, a response containing access_token, expires_in and refresh_token therefore loses its expiry and refresh token. Zoom subsequently calculates an invalid expiry, and Office 365 cannot retain the returned expiry. Define explicit response fields or use an appropriate catchall/passthrough schema.

The golden comment says this throws a runtime error, while the candidate says it creates literal "[object Object]" keys that strip fields. The predicted consequence differs, but the underlying bug is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

refreshOAuthTokens treats its third argument as a user ID and sends it as calcomUserId, but Bigin passes credentialId. Credential IDs and user IDs are unrelated, so a sync endpoint will either fail to locate the account or return another user's token when the numbers happen to match. false_positives.candidate:
Import Prisma before using the new credential update

The new refresh path calls prisma.credential.update, but this file has no prisma import or declaration. This fails TypeScript checking and, if executed without checking, throws ReferenceError after Salesforce successfully returns a token. An external app store supplying only an access token cannot keep this integration working, and it is not the source of truth for refreshes as it is for the other integrations. The refresh request sends appSlug="zoomvideo", while the Zoom OAuth callback creates credentials with appId="zoom" and the new webhook resolves applications by their actual slug. Previously, database reminder deletions were included in the awaited Promise.all. The handler can now report a successful cancellation while its cancelled flags or unscheduled-reminder deletions are still pending; in a serverless request those operations can be interrupted after the response, leaving reminders eligible to be sent. For example, an email due at 10:10 for a booking cancelled at 10:01 after the 10:00 run will still be sent. At 10:15, scheduleEmailReminders deletes the expired reminder before attempting cancellation, so it never contacts SendGrid for that email. Reminders close to their send time need an immediate cancellation path.

Passing immediateDelete=true cancels every old rescheduled-booking email immediately in SendGrid, including emails scheduled days ahead. Those cancellations remain pending until their original send dates and consume the same 100-pending-cancellation limit identified in this PR. Once that limit is reached, the helper catches the failure without setting cancelled=true, leaving the old reminder scheduled with no cron retry. Rescheduling therefore still exhausts the cancellation quota and sends obsolete reminders.

Isolate cancellation failures and persist each successful cancellation

The entire cancellation loop shares one try/catch, and its Prisma deletes are lazy promises executed only after every SendGrid request succeeds. If any request fails, all later reminders are skipped and none of the earlier successful cancellations are removed from the database. A persistent failure can consequently block unrelated cancellations on every run until their emails are sent. Handle errors per reminder and execute each database deletion after its corresponding successful cancellation.

This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

Normalize guest addresses before checking the blacklist

BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS entries are lowercased, but incoming guest addresses are compared without lowercasing them. Zod's email validation accepts uppercase characters, so submitting a mixed-case version of a blacklisted address bypasses the blacklist and receives an invitation. Normalize incoming addresses before applying the blacklist and existing-attendee checks.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: the blacklist entries are lowercased but the incoming guest emails are not, so a mixed-case blacklisted address bypasses the check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorize team administrators or owners rather than requiring both

The isTeamAdminOrOwner check combines isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner with &&. This requires the caller to satisfy both role checks instead of either one. A team administrator who is neither the organizer nor an attendee is consequently rejected with FORBIDDEN when trying to add guests to a team booking. Combine the role checks with OR.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: the admin/owner permission check uses && when it should use ||, so it wrongly requires a user to hold both roles.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Deduplicate incoming guests on the server

uniqueGuests only removes addresses already present in the booking; it does not remove repetitions within the submitted guests array. The server schema accepts duplicate addresses, so a direct API request containing the same new address twice passes validation and sends both entries to createMany. This can create duplicate attendees and duplicate invitations despite the UI's uniqueness validation. Enforce uniqueness server-side before inserting attendees.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: uniqueGuests doesn't dedupe repeated emails within the input array, so createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Respect event-type email suppression when adding guests

sendAddGuestsEmails unconditionally emails the organizer and every attendee, unlike the adjacent scheduling and location-change flows that honor disableStandardEmails metadata. The handler also does not pass event-type metadata to this function. Adding a guest therefore sends standard emails even for event types whose host or attendee notifications have explicitly been disabled. Accept the metadata and apply the existing host and attendee suppression checks.
true_positives.reasoning: Both say sendAddGuestsEmails ignores the disableStandardEmails metadata, so emails still go out to hosts and attendees when standard emails are disabled. This is the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Update calendars using the booking organizer's credentials

The handler allows attendees and team administrators to add guests, but constructs EventManager with the caller and the caller's credentials. When the caller is not the booking organizer, those credentials do not authorize updates to the organizer's existing calendar event. Guests are already persisted before this update is attempted, so the booking can gain attendees while the actual calendar invitation remains unchanged or the mutation fails. Use the booking organizer's credentials for the calendar update.

Handle seated bookings through the seat allocation flow

This mutation accepts seated bookings but inserts ordinary attendees without checking seatsPerTimeSlot or creating seat references. The new action is also exposed for these bookings. As a result, callers can add attendees beyond the configured capacity, and those attendees have no seat reference for the seat-specific cancellation and rescheduling links used by the booking UI. Either reject seated bookings in this flow or allocate guests through the seat-booking logic with capacity checks and seat references.

Reject guest additions to inactive or unconfirmed bookings

The handler checks permissions and guest addresses but never checks the booking status. An authorized caller can invoke it for a cancelled or rejected booking, after which new guests receive AttendeeScheduledEmail and existing attendees receive an ICS request marked CONFIRMED. Pending bookings can likewise receive confirmed invitations without being approved. Validate that the booking is in a supported status before inserting guests or issuing calendar updates and notifications.

Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is not atomic

The backup-code list is read before validation and then overwritten with an update conditioned only on the user ID. Two concurrent login requests can read the same list, validate the same code, and both successfully authenticate, violating the single-use guarantee. Concurrent requests using different codes can also overwrite each other's removals, making a consumed code usable again. Consume codes atomically, such as through a conditional update against the previously read ciphertext whose success is checked before granting access.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: concurrent logins with the same backup code both pass validation before the write-back, which breaks the one-time-use guarantee.

false_positives.candidate:
A dummy TOTP value lets backup-code login bypass the password

Password verification above this branch runs only when credentials.totpCode is empty. A caller can therefore submit an account's email, a valid backupCode, and any nonempty totpCode (for example, "x") without supplying the password. This new branch accepts the backup code and never validates the supplied TOTP, so authentication succeeds with only the recovery code instead of both authentication factors. Ensure password authentication for CAL accounts cannot be skipped by supplying an unverified TOTP alongside a backup code.

Identity-provider users cannot access backup-code recovery

When totpEmail is present after Google or SAML authentication, the page renders ExternalTotpFooter instead of TwoFactorFooter. Only TwoFactorFooter exposes the Lost access button, so these users can never reach the backup-code input. This affects accounts that generated backup codes while using CAL authentication and subsequently switched to an identity provider: the authentication callbacks retain their enabled 2FA and backup codes. The server also rejects a third-party account's backup-only submission because its identity-provider guards require totpCode. Provide a recovery route for this flow and make the server accept its backup-code authentication; otherwise users with valid saved codes remain locked out after losing their authenticator.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

Self-hosted or other non-billing deployments therefore create organizations without the slug needed to identify their organization URLs. Preserve the previous non-billing slug assignment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

Every host's credential receives the entire destinationCalendar array. Only the Google adapter selects a destination by credentialId; Office365, Lark, and BaseCalendarService all use the first element. Consequently, a secondary host's Office365 or Lark credential attempts to create an event in the main host's calendar, typically failing with an inaccessible or invalid calendar ID. true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment is about an interface signature mismatch: Lark and Office365 declare createEvent without the credentialId parameter. The candidate is about runtime behavior: those adapters use the first destinationCalendar element instead of selecting by credentialId. The two are related, since both note that Lark and Office365 don't handle credentialId, and the candidate's suggestion to make all adapters select by credentialId implies they need the parameter. However, the candidate never mentions the signature or interface contract violation. It is partially overlapping.

false_positives.candidate:
Guard the missing destination calendar before checking Google Meet

When destinationCalendar is null, undefined, or empty, destructuring produces an undefined mainHostDestinationCalendar. For a Google Meet location, accessing its integration throws instead of falling back to Cal Video as before. Booking creation therefore fails for event types that still select Google Meet after their destination calendar has been removed. Use optional chaining here.

Preserve credential IDs on video references

This change sets credentialId to undefined for every non-calendar result, discarding the credential ID returned by video meeting creation. handleCancelBooking only deletes a video meeting when its booking reference has a credentialId. Newly created Zoom and other dedicated video bookings will therefore leave their remote meetings active after cancellation. Preserve result.credentialId for video references.

Initialize the destination array before adding collective hosts

If neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, evt.destinationCalendar is initialized to null. The optional push then silently discards all destination calendars collected from the other collective hosts. Those hosts receive no calendar events even when their calendars are connected. Initialize an empty array and append the collected destinations regardless of whether the organizer has one.

Retain destination selection for calendars without a credential ID

This new lookup cannot match such a destination to the numeric credentialId passed to createEvent, so Google always inserts into primary rather than the configured externalId. true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawned workers fail the multiprocessing.Process type check

Workers are created using multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, whose SpawnProcess class is not a subclass of the default-context multiprocessing.Process class. Consequently, this isinstance check is false for production workers, so an unhealthy worker is never killed before its replacement starts.
